overview: The file chiefly documents the Japanese colonial government’s extension of economic planning over Taiwan’s sugar industry in October 1939. A despatch from American Vice Consul John K. Emmerson reports the Taiwan Sugar Industry Ordinance, explains its relationship to rice control and imperial trade policy, and encloses a translated résumé detailing licensing, territorial, acreage, price, production, sales, and accounting controls. The final page is an earlier and apparently unrelated 1932 State Department memorandum concerning regulations intended to prevent Taiwan-registered fishing vessels from violating Philippine territorial waters.

subfiles.title: Despatch on government control of Taiwan’s sugar industry
subfiles.from: John K. Emmerson, American Vice Consul, Taihoku
subfiles.about: Reports the promulgation and purposes of the Taiwan Sugar Industry Ordinance of October 3, 1939.
subfiles.summary: Emmerson reports that the Taiwan Government General has brought the island’s sugar industry under comprehensive control, complementing the Rice Control Ordinance of May 1939. The new system requires licensing and permits the government to regulate cane acreage, purchasing prices, and crushing periods. Statements by Governor General Kobayashi and Director General Morioka present the measure as necessary to balance rice and sugar production, secure imperial supplies, and expand exports to China, Manchukuo, and other markets within and outside the yen bloc.

subfiles.title: Okuda’s résumé of the Taiwan Sugar Industry Ordinance
subfiles.from: Tatsuro Okuda; translated by C. Matsuo
subfiles.about: Summarizes the principal regulatory provisions imposed on Taiwan’s sugar manufacturers and cane-growing territories.
subfiles.summary: Okuda explains that manufacturers of centrifugal and native brown sugar must be licensed and must obtain permission for major organizational or equipment changes. The ordinance preserves designated cane territories while regulating cane movement, acreage, buying prices, crushing schedules, production and sales agreements, company accounts, and uses of sugar cane. It authorizes suspension, restriction, and penalties for violations, extends control to primitive mills, and limits recognition of territories for semi-modern mills to five years.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Taiwan fishing-vessel regulations
subfiles.from: U.S. Department of State, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Transmits information about new Taiwan regulations intended to reduce incursions by Japanese fishing vessels into Philippine waters.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum describes an attached letter from the American consul at Taihoku to the Governor General of the Philippine Islands. It states that new Taiwan Government General regulations should reduce violations of Philippine territorial waters and require identifying markings that would assist Philippine customs authorities. The writer expects the measures to improve relations between Japan and the Philippines; the referenced letter itself is not present in the supplied pages.

interest: The 1939 material offers a concise view of how Japan’s colonial administration coordinated Taiwan’s two leading crops and subordinated growers, manufacturers, prices, and land use to imperial supply and export objectives. Okuda’s enclosure is especially useful because it gathers the ordinance’s operational provisions into a compact contemporary summary. The stray 1932 memorandum is also revealing archivally: despite the agricultural file title, it preserves evidence about fisheries enforcement, maritime boundaries, vessel identification, and Japanese-Philippine relations.
